clue.text: See 26
Look up in city — see a star

indicators.note: the reversed look is placed within the name of the city

parts.note: Paris is the French capital city

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A tourist is told to gaze upward in a city to spot a star in the night sky.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reads the look backwards, and 'in' sets that turned word just after the capital's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris is the Pole Star, the bright star above the north celestial pole.

clue.text: Husband ensconced in pleasant nook

indicators.note: to be ensconced is to be settled snugly inside something, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: nice means pleasant

explanation.surface: A husband is settled comfortably in a cosy corner of the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a recess or small corner, a synonym for a nook.

clue.text: Most mean to install an audio receiver in comfy home

indicators.note: the receiver is installed within the comfy home, so it goes inside

parts.note: a nest is a snug, comfortable home
the ear is the organ that receives sound

explanation.surface: Someone very stingy decides to fit a sound system in their cosy house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most mean' suggests average, but near can mean stingy, so the superlative means the stingiest.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old word for stingy or tight-fisted, so the superlative means the stingiest.

clue.text: About to leave French city, one originally providing base

indicators.note: originally says the one comes first, at the start of the word

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the word for about departs from the city's name, so it is removed

parts.note: Grenoble is a city in the French Alps
re means about or concerning, as in business letters

explanation.surface: Someone leaving a French city, the first one to do so, ends up providing a base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to leave' takes the word for about out of the Alpine city, and 'originally' puts the one at the very start.
explanation.definitionFit: Base and ignoble both mean dishonourable, lacking in moral worth.

clue.text: Author in terrible rage about meat too raw to eat?

indicators.note: the rearranged rage goes around the meat and the unripe word
terrible signals that the letters of rage are thrown into disorder

parts.note: ham is a meat
green fruit is unripe, too raw to be eaten

explanation.surface: Someone flies into a terrible rage over meat served too raw to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges RAGE into GRA...E, which goes 'about' HAM plus GREEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Greene was the English novelist whose works give this puzzle its theme.

clue.text: Going off or about to come back?

definitions.meaning: milk or food that is starting to sour is said to be going off
a tide or a traveller about to turn round and return is at the turning point

explanation.definitionFit: Milk that is souring is on the turn, and the tide on the turn is about to come back in.

clue.text: Aperture that's clear embedded in sealant

indicators.note: one piece is set into the middle of the other

parts.note: lute is a clay or cement used to seal joints
net means clear, as in net profit after deductions

explanation.surface: A clear opening is set into a layer of sealing compound.
explanation.walkthrough: Lute is a sealing paste, and net (clear of deductions) as in net pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunette is a crescent-shaped opening or window in a vault or dome.

clue.text: Regret Arcadia being spoilt by wealthy patrons

indicators.note: the two words are spoilt, broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone laments that an idyllic Arcadia has been ruined by rich customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being spoilt' rearranges the letters of REGRET and ARCADIA together.
explanation.definitionFit: The carriage trade is business from the rich, once those who arrived by carriage.

clue.text: A talk at university? Smart chap cuts the second half

indicators.note: the second half is cut away, so only the first four of the eight letters stay

parts.note: a lecture is a talk given at university

explanation.surface: A clever fellow shortens a university talk by half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuts the second half' keeps the first four letters of A LECTURE, eight letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart alec is a know-all, so Alec is the chap the phrase calls smart.

clue.text: Very hard worker in a pit given notice first

indicators.note: first says the notice comes at the front of the word

parts.note: ad is short for advertisement, a notice

indicators.note: the worker is put within a pit

parts.note: a mine is a pit dug for coal
ant is the crossword worker, from worker ants

explanation.surface: A labourer down a pit is given advance notice of something very tough.
explanation.walkthrough: ANT goes 'in' A MINE to give AMANTINE, with AD placed 'first'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamantine describes something unbreakable, like the legendary hard stone adamant.

clue.text: See 6
Chemicals found in regions? Not initially, man admitted

indicators.note: the man is let into the trimmed word for regions
the first letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: areas are regions
gent is short for gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: Chemicals turn up in certain parts of the country after a man is let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not initially' drops the first letter of the word for regions, and 'admitted' lets the man into what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Reagents are substances used to bring about chemical reactions, a kind of chemical.

clue.text: See 26
See how lady without line plastered cosmetic

indicators.note: plastered means drunk, so the letters are reeling into a new order
the lady is left without a letter

explanation.surface: Look how a drunk woman has smeared her make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops L from LADY to leave ADY, and 'plastered' rearranges SEE HOW with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eye shadow is make-up applied to the eyelids, a cosmetic.

clue.text: It's like an American to give up — English will get stuck in!

indicators.note: the letter for English is lodged inside the word for giving up

parts.note: to quit is to give up

explanation.surface: An exasperated American wants to give up, while the English carry on doggedly.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to Greene's novel The Quiet American, so the word sits beside American.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's novel The Quiet American makes this adjective the one that describes its American.

clue.text: Tender chest though cold has been shifted

indicators.note: the letter for cold is moved out, so it is removed

parts.note: a coffer is a chest for valuables
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A sore chest, though the cold has now cleared up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like sore, but as a verb it means to put forward.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender a bid or resignation is to offer it.

clue.text: Genevan chess player

definitions.meaning: the doctor of Geneva in Greene's novel Doctor ... of Geneva
Bobby ... was the American world chess champion

explanation.definitionFit: Greene's Doctor Fischer lives in Geneva, and Bobby Fischer was a world chess champion.

clue.text: See 26
Foolish talk from the Yorkshire and England player of yesteryear

parts.note: in Yorkshire dialect the is clipped to t'
Chris Waddle was an England footballer of the 1980s and 1990s

explanation.surface: Nonsense spoken by an old cricketer who played for Yorkshire and England.
explanation.walkthrough: In Yorkshire speech 'the' is cut to t', as in 'on t' moor'. Chris Waddle played football for England and for Sheffield Wednesday, a Yorkshire club.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle is silly, trivial talk or writing, nonsense.

clue.text: Author's creator in the country

definitions.meaning: Greene's novel ... Made Me names the place that made its writer
a country of the United Kingdom

explanation.definitionFit: Greene's novel England Made Me names the country as the maker of its author.

clue.text: Time to have mourning clothes, woollen garments

parts.note: widow's weeds are the black clothes worn in mourning

explanation.surface: It is time to put on black mourning clothes made of wool.
explanation.walkthrough: Weeds, as in widow's weeds, is an old word for mourning dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweeds are clothes made of the rough woollen cloth tweed.

clue.text: One abstaining may find "Cheers!" inappropriate, we gathered

indicators.note: the toast and we are put in an improper arrangement, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A teetotaller, we learn, may think raising a glass to say cheers unsuitable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inappropriate' rearranges CHEERS with WE; 'gathered' means we understood.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who eschews something avoids it, so one who abstains from it.

clue.text: Declare 50 on in game with Nos 1 and 3 out

indicators.note: the number and the cricket word go inside what remains of the game
the first and third letters of the word are taken out

parts.note: a game is any match or sport
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
on is the leg side in cricket

explanation.surface: A player declares at 50 in a game, with the first and third batsmen out.
explanation.walkthrough: GAME without letters 1 and 3 leaves AE; L plus LEG go 'in'. In cricket the on side is also called the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: To allege is to declare or assert something, usually without proof.

clue.text: The author's one taking all unexpectedly

definitions.text: The author's one taking all unexpectedly

parts.words: The author's one taking all unexpectedly
parts.note: points to Greene's novella whose title says the one who should fail wins everything

explanation.definitionFit: Greene's Loser Takes All is about a man who unexpectedly wins at the casino.

clue.text: See pained 12 halt — discontentedness possibly produced by this introduction?

indicators.note: possibly signals that all these letters may be rearranged

parts.note: 12 across is the second half of the author's name, the surname

explanation.surface: A pained reader is told to stop being discontented with the opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges SEE PAINED, GREENE, HALT and DISCONTENTEDNESS, thirty-five letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue's opening line is its introduction, and this is the long sentence that introduces the puzzle.

clue.text: Climb is said to be painful

indicators.note: said tells us the word is heard spoken, sounding like another

parts.note: sore means painful

explanation.surface: Climbing is said to hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: SORE and SOAR sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To soar is to rise high or climb through the air.

clue.text: Skill shown in front when given female backing

indicators.note: backing puts the female ending at the back of the word

parts.note: the prow is the front of a ship
-ess is the ending that makes a noun female, as in lioness

explanation.surface: Skill is shown in the front line when women back you up.
explanation.walkthrough: -ESS is the suffix that marks a female, as in actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Prowess is great skill or expertise.

clue.text: Philosopher completed article about sin

indicators.note: the completed word and the article go round the word for sin

parts.note: did means completed, as in did the job
to err is to sin
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A philosopher finished an essay on sin.
explanation.walkthrough: DID A goes 'about' ERR to give D-ERR-IDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Derrida was a French philosopher, the founder of deconstruction.
